cases.title: Wide-beam GEO: Arabsat 7B (Badr-8)
cases.summary: A broadcast and trunking satellite at 26 degrees east with a few large shaped beams. Its line of sight is exact. Three of its beams are drawn from Arabsat's own downlink EIRP contours, read on 24 Nov 2026 and redrawn with credit; two beams are also estimated from their names and scored against those contours.

published.label: Ku-band FSS MENA beam
published.source: Arabsat's own downlink EIRP contours for Badr-8 (KML behind the coverage map on the Badr-8 page of arabsat.com), read 24 Nov 2026 and redrawn as facts with credit: the operator's file is not copied
published.uncertainty: As the operator publishes it, with no date or method stated. Downlink only; the uplink beam is not published.

published.label: Ku-band North West Africa beam
published.source: Arabsat's own downlink EIRP contours for Badr-8 (KML behind the coverage map on the Badr-8 page of arabsat.com), read 24 Nov 2026 and redrawn as facts with credit: the operator's file is not copied
published.uncertainty: As the operator publishes it, with no date or method stated. Downlink only; the uplink beam is not published.

published.label: C-band global beam
published.source: Arabsat's own downlink EIRP contours for Badr-8 (KML behind the coverage map on the Badr-8 page of arabsat.com), read 24 Nov 2026 and redrawn as facts with credit: the operator's file is not copied
published.uncertainty: As the operator publishes it, with no date or method stated. Downlink only; the uplink beam is not published.

estimates.label: Ku-band 'MENA' beam, from its name
estimates.area_words: the 22 member states of the Arab League, taken as what 'MENA' means for the Arab League's own operator
estimates.source: Beam name from third-party listings of Badr-8's beams; the country list is Orbit's reading of the name
estimates.uncertainty: A beam name is not a contour: no gain level, and a shaped beam is not an ellipse. Scored below against Arabsat's 43 dBW contour of the same beam; expect errors of hundreds of km.

estimates.label: Ku-band 'North West Africa' beam, from its name
estimates.area_words: the UN's Northern Africa without Egypt and Sudan, plus its Western Africa
estimates.source: Beam name as in Arabsat's own contour file names; the country list is Orbit's reading of the name
estimates.uncertainty: A beam name is not a contour: no gain level, and a shaped beam is not an ellipse. Scored below against Arabsat's 43 dBW contour of the same beam; expect errors of hundreds of km.

notes: Airbus, which built the satellite, says it provides connectivity over Europe, the Middle East, Africa and central Asia, in C and Ku band. That is nearly everything in its line of sight, which is why the line of sight alone says little about where a beam points.

Arabsat publishes contour files for this satellite behind the Badr-8 page of its website (KML, downlink EIRP in dBW: six Ku-band beams and a C-band global beam). They were read on 24 Nov 2026 for where the contours run, and are redrawn here with credit; no file is copied. Arabsat's terms ask that its site not be linked without consent, so it is credited by name only.
Uplink and downlink beams are different shapes on most satellites. Only downlink beams are named in the public material found.

cases.title: High-throughput GEO: KA-SAT
cases.summary: A Ka-band satellite at 9 degrees east that covers Europe and the Mediterranean with about 82 small spot beams instead of a few large ones. The public record gives the number of spots, a round figure for their size and the region in words. Where each spot sits is on the operator's map, which may be linked but not redrawn.

estimates.label: One spot beam, for scale
estimates.source: Eutelsat's own 2012 presentation gives about 300 km across for each spot; another technical page gives 0.5 degrees
estimates.uncertainty: A round published figure with no gain level; sources give 250 to 300 km. The aim point is an example, not a real beam centre, so this shows the size of a spot and nothing about its place.

estimates.label: Whole service area, from the words 'Europe and the Mediterranean Basin'
estimates.area_words: the mainland and nearby islands of 48 European and Mediterranean countries (between 12 west and 45 east, 27 and 72 north), as Orbit read the phrase
estimates.source: Service area in words from public descriptions of KA-SAT; the country list is Orbit's reading
estimates.uncertainty: An outline around named countries. Spot-beam satellites leave gaps inside such an outline (sea, desert, unserved countries), which this cannot show. Not checked against any published contour.

notes: Sources give 82 or 83 spot beams; two of the beams are said to be alternatives to each other.

KA-SAT was Eutelsat's and is now owned by Viasat (through Euro Broadband Infrastructure). Blackout's register reaches it through Skylogic's networks, which run its gateways. A network number therefore does not name the satellite's owner.
On a spot-beam satellite a user's outage can come from one spot or one gateway. Neither can be placed from public data without the operator's beam map.
No contour for this satellite was found in a public filing: it is not US-licensed, and ITU's beam data needs a login that Orbit does not use.

notes: Schedule S words the beams' areas as "North America coverages" and "CONUS coverage", each "with reflector RPM capability of plus minus 8.7" degrees east-west and north-south.

The Ku-band beams (contiguous US, North, East and South Pacific; 14.0-14.5 GHz up, 11.7-12.2 GHz down) belong to the Horizons-4 payload. The engineering statement says Intelsat sought FCC authority for C band only, that the Ku payload is licensed by Japan and would seek US market access separately, and that the filing describes the whole spacecraft "for administrative ease".

The engineering statement names the Pacific beams' areas only as the "North Pacific area", "East Pacific area" and "South Pacific area", so they have no service-area estimates. A May 2023 supplement to the filing says every Ku-band beam is steerable.
The East and South Pacific beams' filed outlines each include a small separate contour around Hawaii, drawn as filed. The North Pacific beam covers Hawaii in its main outline.
Only the downlink diagrams are drawn. The East and South Pacific uplink diagrams (EPHU, SPHU) have the same outlines as their downlinks; the North Pacific uplink (NPVU) differs slightly.
The beam Schedule S calls "CONUS coverage" also reaches Alaska and Hawaii in its filed -2 and -4 dB contours, so the service-area estimate, drawn round the contiguous states only, misses those parts.
This filing's diagrams came in a later attachment (G-37new mdb 2023.zip), not with the application form.

The filing's database is locked against the Access engine; Orbit reads its diagrams from the file's pages (orbit.footprint.gims_long_blocks), checked byte for byte against Galaxy 34's diagrams, which the engine does open.

notes: Schedule S words the Western Arc area as "North America including Alaska and Hawaii; Central America; and the Caribbean", with a reflector repointable by plus or minus 10 degrees east-west and 8 degrees north-south, so the filed outline is one pointing, not the only one.
Schedule S calls the Ku-band downlink area only "Ku band wide beam", so that beam has no service-area estimate. Its uplink is worded "Contiguous United States; Central America; and Caribbean".

Not drawn: the C-band hemispheric beams (CHHD, CHVD, CHHU, CHVU). Schedule S words their area as "North America including Alaska and Hawaii; Central America; the Caribbean; South America and Western Europe", and the filing's engineering statement calls them "Hemi Beam 45W". The filed diagrams put the peak in the south-east Pacific (boresight about 127 W, 26 S, downlink; 131 W, 30 S, uplink), with most of the -2 and -4 dB outlines over open ocean west of South America. Orbit found no reading of the filing that puts them on the named area, so they are left out until one is found. The engineering statement names the uplink beams "Hemi Beam 45W". On 25 Nov 2026 LyngSat and Satbeams listed only a North America C-band beam in use on Galaxy 36, and Intelsat's fact sheets now redirect to SES, which publishes no Galaxy 36 coverage map, so no public map shows where the hemispheric beam points from 89 degrees west.

The filing has a second database, "new at 45.mdb", holding the same 16 diagrams with every longitude moved 44 degrees east (the beams as they would fall from 45 degrees west). Its hemispheric beam still peaks over the Pacific, off Chile. It is not drawn.

In this database the Ku-band downlink diagrams (KUHD, K1HD) are marked R (receive), while Schedule S lists them as transmit beams. Orbit follows Schedule S. The C-band rows are marked as Schedule S has them.

The FCC's earth-station file has 86 current licences naming Galaxy 28, the satellite Galaxy 36 replaced at the same slot, and 1 naming Galaxy 36. Only the Galaxy 36 licence is drawn: names are matched exactly.

The filing's database is locked against the Access engine; Orbit reads its diagrams from the file's pages (orbit.footprint.gims_long_blocks), checked byte for byte against Galaxy 34's diagrams, which the engine does open.

notes: The licence for C band at 93.1 degrees west is SAT-MOD-20230517-00112, granted in March 2025. Its Schedule S names a GIMS database ("G-35 C,ku,ka .mdb") that is not among the filing's public attachments. The diagrams drawn here come from the database attached to Intelsat's April 2025 application to add Ku and Ka band (SAT-MOD-20250417-00104), which the FCC lists as pending review. Both Schedule S give the C-band beams the same peak gains (29.03 dBi down, 30.52 dBi up).

Schedule S words both C-band beams' areas as "North America including Alaska and Hawaii; Central America; and the Caribbean", each with a reflector repointable by plus or minus 10 degrees east-west and 8 degrees north-south. The spacecraft can also bias its whole platform by 3.5 degrees east-west and 1.0 degree north-south, so the filed outlines are one pointing, not the only one.

The Ku-band beam K1HD (11.7-12.2 GHz down) is part of the pending application and starts switched off. Its area is worded "Contiguous United States; Central America; and Caribbean". The same database's Ka-band diagrams (KALD, KARD, A1LD, A1RD, A2LD, A2RD), worded "Contiguous United States" on a reflector fixed to the platform, are not drawn.

After the C-band transition, Intelsat seeks to downlink only 4000-4200 MHz in the contiguous United States and the whole 3700-4200 MHz band outside it, apart from telemetry, tracking and command. The outlines show where the beams reach, not which part of the band is used where.

The filing's database is locked against the Access engine; Orbit reads its diagrams from the file's pages (orbit.footprint.gims_long_blocks), checked byte for byte against Galaxy 34's diagrams, which the engine does open.

cases.title: High-throughput GEO: Telstar 19 VANTAGE

notes: Telesat publishes a downlink (EIRP) and an uplink (G/T) contour set for each beam, and they are not the same shape. The scores below show how far apart they run.

The FCC filing gives each beam's maximum EIRP and G/T in its text, which put the filed contours (in dB below the peak) into dBW and dB/K for the check. It gives no peak antenna gain, so no beam can be drawn as a circle from it.

Telesat's map draws one outline round neighbouring spots at its lower levels. A single filed spot covers only part of such an outline, so the check uses spot S5 over the Amazon, which stands alone at every level, and spot S2 at its top level only.
Of the filing's beams, six Ku-band spot diagrams and one Ka-band diagram are stored whole in its database and could be read; the rest are split across database pages.

cases.title: LEO constellation: Starlink
cases.summary: A low-orbit constellation has no fixed footprint. From orbits alone, the only thing that can be computed is how many satellites stand high enough in the sky at each latitude. Where service is actually sold and switched on is set by licences, gateways and the operator, and has to come from what the operator publishes or from terminals seen in use.
cases.tle_source: CelesTrak, Starlink group (element sets from the 18th Space Defense Squadron)

measured.label: Terminals seen in use: RIPE Atlas probes connected through Starlink's network (AS14593), at the places their hosts report
measured.uncertainty: A lower bound from volunteers, mostly in North America and Europe. Places are reported by each host and may be offset on purpose. No probe says nothing about no service.

notes: Service angles as the FCC authorised them: user terminals work down to 25 degrees above the horizon below 62 degrees north, and down to 5 degrees at and above it (FCC DA 24-1193). SpaceX has asked for 20 degrees on its 400 to 500 km shells; no grant was found.

Serving satellites are taken as those between 425 and 600 km on near-circular orbits. The FCC's January 2026 order (DA 26-36) also authorises shells at 340 to 365 km, and the element sets hold about 800 satellites near 350 to 375 km. Whether those are serving or still raising cannot be told from the orbits, so they are left out and counted under Other.

Starlink's IP geolocation feed is not drawn. It lists 238 countries and territories, including ones where Starlink has no licence, and SpaceX does not say what a row means, so it is not a service-area map.
Not shown, because it is not geometry: which countries have service (the operator's availability map says), where gateways are, and how much capacity a cell has.
